The number of hours the vehicle was instrumented with a data logger within each hour and day type was also tracked and is denoted the “instrumented hours.” The instrumented hours serve as a normalization factor when the data are aggregated across vehicles, such that each vehicle is weighted according to its usage rate, rather than how long the vehicle was instrumented or by equally weighing each vehicle. This approach is also referred to as the “normalized sum over sum” approach used to calculate representative activity distributions (Zhang et al. 2021). When a subscript has an equality, it means that the identifier is fixed across the sum, and the equation is performed iteratively for all possible values (e.g., calculation is run separately for each of the 24 hours in a day, for the two day types, the four road types, and each source type). Because the equation is performed across different groups of vehicles within each source type, each term contributing to the sum will have a different vehicle ID, and the vehicle ID is not fixed in the equation. The speed distribution equation is calculated separately for each source type, road type, day type, and hour of the day.
